plain_text: Spot the signs and get advice for living with this 'silent' bone disease
semantic_text: Spot the signs and get advice for living with this 'silent' bone disease

plain_text:
Did you know that our bones are living tissue? To keep them
strong, our bodies break down old bone and replace them
with new bone. When we are young, we build more bone
than we break down. But as we get older, bone can break down
more often than it gets replaced. This can lead to osteoporosis.
semantic_text: Did you know that our bones are living tissue? To keep them strong, our bodies break down old bone and replace them with new bone. When we are young, we build more bone than we break down. But as we get older, bone can break down more often than it gets replaced. This can lead to osteoporosis.

plain_text:
Osteoporosis can develop if your bone mass decreases or the
structure of your bones changes. Osteoporosis makes your bones
weak and more likely to fracture (break).
semantic_text: Osteoporosis can develop if your bone mass decreases or the structure of your bones changes. Osteoporosis makes your bones weak and more likely to fracture (break).

plain_text:
Osteoporosis is called a “silent” disease because it doesn’t show
any obvious symptoms. Many people do not know they have it until
they break a bone after a minor injury or movement. Something
as simple as falling from standing height, bending, lifting, or even
intense coughing may cause a fracture. Osteoporosis can develop in
any bone, but it’s most common in the bones of your hips, wrists,
and vertebrae in the spine.
semantic_text: Osteoporosis is called a “silent” disease because it doesn’t show any obvious symptoms. Many people do not know they have it until they break a bone after a minor injury or movement. Something as simple as falling from standing height, bending, lifting, or even intense coughing may cause a fracture. Osteoporosis can develop in any bone, but it’s most common in the bones of your hips, wrists, and vertebrae in the spine.

plain_text:
While anyone can develop osteoporosis, the risk increases as you
get older. Osteoporosis is more common in people with any of
these risk factors:
semantic_text: While anyone can develop osteoporosis, the risk increases as you get older. Osteoporosis is more common in people with any of these risk factors:

plain_text:
■ Sex. Women are more likely to have osteoporosis than men,
especially after menopause. White and Asian women are
at the highest risk. African American and Hispanic women
are at a slightly lower risk. While men are less likely to have
osteoporosis, White men are at a higher risk than other groups
of their sex.
semantic_text: ■ Sex. Women are more likely to have osteoporosis than men, especially after menopause. White and Asian women are at the highest risk. African American and Hispanic women are at a slightly lower risk. While men are less likely to have osteoporosis, White men are at a higher risk than other groups of their sex.

plain_text:
■ Age. As you age, you lose more bone than you build. Women over
age 65 are recommended to get screened for osteoporosis by their
health provider. There are no official screening recommendations
for men, but their risk increases after age 70.
*
semantic_text: ■ Age. As you age, you lose more bone than you build. Women over age 65 are recommended to get screened for osteoporosis by their health provider. There are no official screening recommendations for men, but their risk increases after age 70. *

plain_text:
■ Family history. Having a parent with osteoporosis or hip fracture
increases risk.
semantic_text: ■ Family history. Having a parent with osteoporosis or hip fracture increases risk.

plain_text:
■ Body type. Being slim or thin-boned increases risk because there
is less bone to lose.
semantic_text: ■ Body type. Being slim or thin-boned increases risk because there is less bone to lose.

plain_text:
■ Hormones. Hormone levels can affect risk for both men and
women. Low estrogen levels in women due to menopause,
hormone disorders, or extreme physical activity can weaken
bones. Low levels of testosterone in men also raises their risk for
osteoporosis.
semantic_text: ■ Hormones. Hormone levels can affect risk for both men and women. Low estrogen levels in women due to menopause, hormone disorders, or extreme physical activity can weaken bones. Low levels of testosterone in men also raises their risk for osteoporosis.

plain_text: ■ Nutrition. A diet low in calcium, vitamin D, or protein can raise risk.
semantic_text: ■ Nutrition. A diet low in calcium, vitamin D, or protein can raise risk.

plain_text:
■ Lifestyle factors. These include heavy alcohol use, smoking, not
being physically active, or being on bedrest for extended periods of
time can all raise risk.
semantic_text: ■ Lifestyle factors. These include heavy alcohol use, smoking, not being physically active, or being on bedrest for extended periods of time can all raise risk.

plain_text:
■ Medications. Long-term use of some medications may increase
risk. These include corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitors,
and medicines to treat epilepsy. Some cancer medications and
glucocorticoid steroids can also increase risk.
semantic_text: ■ Medications. Long-term use of some medications may increase risk. These include corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitors, and medicines to treat epilepsy. Some cancer medications and glucocorticoid steroids can also increase risk.

plain_text:
■ Medical conditions. Some medical conditions increase risk,
including:
semantic_text: ■ Medical conditions. Some medical conditions increase risk, including:

plain_text:
– Endocrine diseases
– Certain digestive diseases, such as IBS
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Certain types of cancer
– HIV
– Anorexia nervosa
semantic_text: – Endocrine diseases – Certain digestive diseases, such as IBS – Rheumatoid arthritis – Certain types of cancer – HIV – Anorexia nervosa

plain_text:
A health care provider can usually diagnose osteoporosis with a
routine screening. They may ask you about your medical and family
history and whether you have ever broken a bone. They may also want
to know if you have lost height or weight or if you are losing muscle
strength. Talk to your doctor if your posture, balance, and gait (how
you walk) have changed.
semantic_text: A health care provider can usually diagnose osteoporosis with a routine screening. They may ask you about your medical and family history and whether you have ever broken a bone. They may also want to know if you have lost height or weight or if you are losing muscle strength. Talk to your doctor if your posture, balance, and gait (how you walk) have changed.

plain_text:
The most common test for osteoporosis is a bone mineral density
test, which measures how strong your bones are and predicts your risk
of bone fractures.
semantic_text: The most common test for osteoporosis is a bone mineral density test, which measures how strong your bones are and predicts your risk of bone fractures.

plain_text:
If you have the disease, your doctor will likely recommend treatment
designed to slow or stop bone loss and help prevent fractures.
semantic_text: If you have the disease, your doctor will likely recommend treatment designed to slow or stop bone loss and help prevent fractures.

plain_text:
They may recommend eating a balanced diet with enough calcium,
vitamin D, and protein. They may also recommend other lifestyle
changes or prescribe medicine to slow bone loss or rebuild bone.
Medications can cause side effects, so talk to your doctor or
pharmacist if you have questions about what you're taking.
semantic_text: They may recommend eating a balanced diet with enough calcium, vitamin D, and protein. Medications can cause side effects, so talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions about what you're taking.

plain_text:
The inside of a bone looks similar to a honeycomb. When someone
has osteoporosis, their bones become weaker as the “walls” of the
honeycomb get smaller. The spaces between the bone grow larger,
and the outer shell of the bone also gets thinner. This all works
together to weaken the bone.
